title: Being-time
hookLine: Dogen: time isn't something you pass through; you are time

cards: Where did this morning go? We talk about time like a river, with us on the bank watching hours float away. We spend it, save it, waste it, kill it, run out of it.
Time is outside us, and we're the ones it happens to. Dogen wrote an essay that turns this around.
Readers of Dogen explain that he took an ordinary Japanese word meaning something like sometimes, or at a certain time, and read its two characters side by side: being, and time.

teach.b: The essay is called Uji, being-time. Its claim, put plainly: time is not a container things sit inside. Things are time, and time is things.

teach.h: PINE IS TIME, BAMBOO IS TIME.
teach.b: The pine tree is time, Dogen says in effect, and the bamboo is time. Mountains are time, oceans are time, and so is the person sitting here. Your life isn't moving through the hours; this breath is the hour.
You cross a river and climb a mountain. Afterward, the river and the mountain seem behind you, gone, and you're up here in the present. That's only one way of seeing it, Dogen says.
The crossing and the climbing were being-time, fully, when they happened, and they don't simply vanish into a back room. In the Genjokoan, in the same collection, he writes about firewood and ash.

teach.h: FIREWOOD HAS ITS PLACE, ASH HAS ITS PLACE.
teach.b: But firewood has its own place as firewood, with a before and an after, and yet cut off from them. Ash has its own place too. Each moment stands complete.
Readers explain this in different ways. Some hear impermanence turned inside out: nothing lasts, so each moment is entire.
Others hear a point for sitting: you can't wait for awakening later, because later isn't a separate place. Either way, the question changes.
Not where did the time go, but what is this time being, right now?

how: Zen students read Dogen's Uji with a teacher, slowly and often more than once, and bring its questions into zazen and into daily work in the temple.

o: Dogen's word for time and being as one thing
a Japanese word for the time left in a life
a Zen rule for spending each hour wisely

p: has its own place, before and after
not simply gone into the past

s: Dogen teaches that time is a container things sit inside
he says things are time and time is things.
in Dogen's picture, firewood simply turns into ash
each has its own place, with a before and an after.
readers explain the Uji essay in different ways
some hear impermanence, others advice for sitting.

games.q: you've crossed the river and climbed the mountain. a friend says, "all that's behind you now, it's gone." what would Dogen say?
o: yes, the past is simply gone
the crossing and the climb were being-time, and don't just vanish
games.why: in Uji, each moment is fully being-time when it happens; it doesn't just disappear into a back room.

practice: Sit, feel the weight in the seat and the air on your skin, and notice when the mind leans forward toward later, or back toward earlier.

Then come to this breath, not one on the way to something, but the whole of what your life is doing right now. If it helps, say silently with the in-breath, this is time, and with the out-breath, this is my life.

wordCard.voice: Being-time. Dogen's word, uji, for time and being as one thing: the pine, the mountain and you, not inside time but as time. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese uji: an everyday word for sometimes, which Dogen read as being and time.

carryVoice: Your line: you are time. Not something time happens to, but this breath, this hour. See you tomorrow.
